text.p: The voluntary euthanasia law in Australia's remote Northern Territory, the first administration in the world to legalise assisted suicide, sets out a detailed series of steps that must be followed to avoid criminal charges.
Local doctor Philip Nitschke said on Thursday he had helped a man with prostate cancer complete the procedure to become the first Australian to end his life under the law.
Here is a brief outline of the steps involved:

-- patients who are over 18, terminally ill and in unbearable pain or suffering must first contact a doctor resident in the Northern Territory and ask for approval for voluntary euthanasia. Only the patient can make the request;

-- if this doctor agrees the patient is eligible, approval must be obtained from a specialist in the particular disease and a psychiatrist must examine the patient to ensure he or she is not suffering from depression and is competent to make decisions. The specialist must also be a resident of Nothern Territory, but the psychiatrist can come from elsewhere in Australia;
-- a seven day cooling-off period follows;
-- after the waiting period, patients must reconfirm their request, and wait at least another 48 hours;
-- if the territory authorities grant final approval, the assisted suicide can take place in the territory at any time the patients choose;
-- the law lists a range of drugs which can be taken orally or by injection. If patients cannot administer the drugs themselves, the doctor is allowed to do so;
-- drugs are administered in two stages. First, a barbiturate sends the patient to sleep within seconds. Then, a muscle-relaxant kills the patient by asphyxiation within minutes;

-- the favoured method at this stage appears to be a computerised system developed by Dr Nitschke that takes the patient through a series of questions before a fatal injection. The final question says: "If you press 'Yes', you will cause a lethal injection to be given within 30 seconds, and you will die. Do you wish to proceed?";
-- the coroner is advised and the death certificate records the patient died by euthanasia, listing the drugs used;
-- the coroner can order an investigation into any death.
